body: 2014 (50th-anniversary) letter: business schools use volatility as a proxy for risk; 'this pedagogic assumption makes for easy teaching, it is dead wrong: Volatility is far from synonymous with risk.' The real risk is loss of purchasing power over the holding period. Caveat stated plainly: 'owning equities for a day or a week or a year is far riskier ... than leaving funds in cash-equivalents', relevant to anyone 'forced to sell securities during depressed markets', and 'any party that might have meaningful near-term needs for funds should keep appropriate sums in Treasuries or insured bank deposits.' For multi-decade investors, 'a diversified equity portfolio, bought over time, will prove far less risky than dollar-based securities.' 2024 letter adds the currency angle: 'Paper money can see its value evaporate if fiscal folly prevails ... Fixed-coupon bonds provide no protection against runaway currency', and Berkshire 'will never prefer ownership of cash-equivalent assets over the ownership of good businesses.' 2008: the 'U.S. Treasury bond bubble of late 2008' - 'Clinging to cash equivalents ... is almost certainly a terrible policy if continued for long.' Actionable for an Indian investor: segregate a 2-3 year cash/FD/liquid-fund need bucket so no equity sale is ever forced; above that, measure risk as permanent loss and real (INR-inflation-adjusted) return, not drawdown size.
title: Buffett 2014: 'Volatility is far from synonymous with risk' - but only for investors with long horizons and no forced selling
